title: Graphs, Not Chains
objective: After this lesson you will be able to model agent work as nodes, edges, and shared state; distinguish chains, graphs, and monolith prompts by control-flow needs; and run a miniature graph runner that mirrors LangGraph semantics.
why: Single prompts answer; agents *work* — triage, look up, decide, draft, get approval, log. Chains force every run down one fixed path; monolith prompts cram five jobs into one breath (Prompt 101 Ch.5 showed why that fails). Graphs express what real support flows are: branches on ticket type, loops on verification failure, gates before money moves. Topology is the first senior decision in agent design.

blocks.text: Nodes do, edges decide, state remembers

A **node** is one unit of work (triage ticket, fetch order, draft reply) — a function of state returning state updates. An **edge** is a transition: fixed (`triage → decide`) or **conditional** (a router function mapping state to the next node). **State** is the shared blackboard every node reads and writes. Runs are walks: start node, follow edges, stop at END. Three concepts compose every agent in this course.

blocks.caption: Nodes, conditional edges, END, checkpointer — the canonical skeleton

blocks.text: Chains, graphs, monoliths: the control-flow test

Fixed sequence, no branches, no loops, no gates → **chain** (simpler, cheaper). Any routing, retry, shared evolving state, or human approval → **graph**. Everything in one giant prompt → **monolith** (the failure mode Prompt 101 decomposed). The test is deletion: remove the router — if nothing breaks, a chain sufficed; if behavior collapses, the topology earns its keep.

rows: No branches, loops, gates, or shared evolving state

blocks.text: Every lesson's practice runs a tiny faithful runner: nodes as `(state) => partialUpdate`, edges as names or router functions, START/END sentinels, step cap against infinite loops, and a trace log. It mirrors LangGraph semantics closely enough that patterns transfer directly — and simply enough to execute in the playground for verification.

blocks.title: Walk the triage graph
blocks.note: Run it: expect '__start__ -> triage | triage -> draft | draft -> __end__' with category shipping and a filled draft. Then change the ticket to 'Delete my account' and re-run: the conditional edge should route to human. Topology steering behavior — the whole course in miniature.

items: Nodes compute (state → updates), edges transition (fixed or router functions), state is the shared blackboard
Chains for fixed sequences; graphs for branches/loops/gates/state; monoliths for prototypes only
Deletion test: remove the router — collapse means the graph earns its keep

exercise.prompt: (a) Run the practice graph on both tickets and record traces + final states. (b) Add a third branch: billing tickets (match /refund|charge|billing/i) routing to a billing node that drafts 'Billing team will review: …'. (c) State which shape (chain/graph/monolith) fits a fixed 3-step FAQ answerer vs this triage system, with the deletion test applied.
hints: Ticket 1 → draft path; ticket 2 → human path. Record both traces exactly — traces are the graph's unit of observable behavior.
Billing node + router branch: order router conditions (billing before other-fallback). Re-run all three tickets: each must hit its own terminal path.
FAQ answerer (retrieve → answer → log, fixed): chain — no router survives deletion analysis. Triage: graph — deleting the router collapses behavior.
exercise.why: Extending the graph (new branch, preserved old paths) practices topology editing safely, and the deletion test converts shape choice from taste to analysis — applied to two systems, not one.
exercise.code: // Branch-addition pattern: node + router case + terminal edge + full re-run.

quiz.q: Triage → decide → draft → log, always in order, no branches. Shape?
options: Chain — fixed sequence, no control-flow needs; routers would be decoration
quiz.explain: Topology follows control flow: nothing branches, loops, or gates, so a chain is simpler, cheaper, and more debuggable.

quiz.q: The deletion test on a triage router shows behavior collapses without it. Meaning?
options: The graph topology earns its keep — routing is load-bearing behavior, not decoration
quiz.explain: Collapse-on-deletion proves the router carries behavior. Surviving deletion proves decoration. Test, don't taste.

quiz.q: Node functions receive state and return…
options: Partial state updates (merged into shared state) — edges, not nodes, decide transitions
quiz.explain: Separation of concerns: nodes compute updates, edges route. A node naming its successor tangles the two and breaks conditional routing.

summary: Nodes update, edges route, state remembers. Chains for fixed flows, graphs for branching/looping/gated work, monoliths for prototypes. The runner is your laboratory for all nine lessons ahead.
next: Walkers need a blackboard that merges sanely: schemas, reducers, and the state design that prevents update chaos. Next: state that survives contact with nodes.
